Article Title: 'Very rare for a kid to tell parents, 'I want to be an athlete'': What India needs for a squash boom
Article Text:
Veer Chotrani (Instagram Photo)

The spark squash needed

The Cornell connection and how it worked

The gaps that still persist

Indian culture is a very academic culture Veer Chotrani

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Veer Chotrani doesn't remember learning to love squash, mainly because there was never a version of his life without it. "I've been around squash for the last 20 years," the 24-year-old told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction. "I was literally born on a squash court, because my father (Manish Chotrani) was a national champion playing for India."He started proper coaching at four, was entering tournaments by six and seven, and grew into a decorated junior career, which included multiple Asian Junior titles and a run as India's junior No. 1 across age categories.It's the kind of story Indian squash needs more of right now, at the exact moment the sport finally has the nation's attention.Just weeks before, 18-year-old Anahat Singh became the first Indian ever to win the World Junior Squash Championship, beating Egypt's Ruqayya Salem in the final to end a 16-year run in which no non-Egyptian had won the girls' title.India's junior boys followed with a bronze. And on the men's PSA tour, Chotrani, currently ranked 38th in the world, sits alongside Abhay Singh (24th), Ramit Tandon, and Velavan Senthilkumar as part of a genuinely unusual cluster: four Indian men inside the world's top 60 simultaneously, for over a year running.Before Anahat, it was the Olympics, Chotrani feels. Squash's inclusion on the program for Los Angeles 2028 reframed the sport overnight, in India specifically."Any sport that makes the Olympics for the first time is going to get a lot more publicity, a lot of eyeballs," he said. "Especially in India, I think the audience here loves champions, in any sport."Anahat Singh's World Junior win landed inside exactly that window, giving Indian squash a headline moment tied directly to Olympic hope."Because squash is an Olympic sport, people have confidence in her getting into the Olympics and doing very well for us," Chotrani said. "I think the Olympics was the main reason squash became what it is today in the last couple of years, and that we've been performing on the world stage."Chotrani's own path off the junior circuit ran through Cornell University, where he studied psychology and trained under David Palmer, the former world No. 1 who remains his coach today."The level of squash in the US collegiate circuit is so high that if you break through and do well there, you have everything you need to give it a shot in professional sport," he said, explaining why three of India's current top-four men have all used the facilities in the US.Fuelling their determination to work harder is the growing rivalry between the two compatriots. Chotrani and Abhay Singh, India's current No. 2 and No. 1, played each other three times last season and split the rivalry 2-1 in Chotrani's favour, including a first-ever meeting in New York, a loss to Abhay in the JSW Open final in Mumbai, and a win at the World Championships in Cairo last May."It's always hard to play someone from your own country, especially in the big tournaments," Chotrani said.What the rivalry does give him, he added, is a target: "It's great to have someone in front of you that you're chasing. But I also have to remember I have Ramit and Velavan right behind me. All four of us are the same level on our best day."For all the momentum, Chotrani is unsentimental about the structural gap still separating India from squash's traditional powers, like Egypt.The problem, in his telling, isn't infrastructure. "We have the courts, we have the facilities," he said. "What we need is the right guidance and the right people to help not just the players playing right now, but the future generation too."The clearest evidence being none of India's top four men actually train inside the country. "Why is that? Because we don't have the right training partners to make us better. We have to be out of India most of the time."He contrasts that with Egypt, squash's dominant nation for decades."A 10-year-old training in a club in Egypt has one of the best players in the world training in that same club to look up to. They have that inspiration, the best coaches, they have everything there," he explained.It's a culture gap as much as a resourcing one, and Chotrani knows it. Government funding has started flowing toward the sport, he agrees, but converting that into an actual home-grown ecosystem, one capable of housing foreign coaches, fitness staff, and sports psychologists under one roof, is the next real project."None of us would have to go abroad to train. That's what everybody wants," he added.There's another obstacle that goes beyond funding and training facilities. It is about what an Indian family expects from a kid. "Indian culture is a very academic culture," Chotrani said with a smile. "Every family wants their kids to have a degree, to pursue medicine or engineering. It's very rare for a kid to tell their parents, 'I want to be an athlete.'"Most junior players in India, he said, follow his own path with strong junior careers, followed by a U.S. degree, after which many simply stop competing. He's careful not to frame that as a failure of will. "It's not wrong at all," he said, pointing to himself, Tandon, and Velavan as proof the two paths aren't mutually exclusive.What happens next, in Chotrani's own assessment, depends less on talent and more on whether the country finally builds somewhere for that talent to stay and train.He remarked, "There are people who've done everything: played junior squash, gotten a degree from a good school, and are still playing on the professional tour right now. You can do that too."
Article Summary: Veer Chotrani is one of four Indian men ranked in the world's top 60. The 24-year-old is currently ranked 38th on the men's PSA tour. He is part of an unusual cluster of Indian men in the top 60 for a year running.

Article Title: 'Difficult for Pakistan to handle': Shoaib Akhtar warns Babar Azam-led side
Article Text:
Babar Azam

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Pakistan fast bowler Shoaib Akhtar has cautioned Pakistan about the challenge awaiting them in England, warning that the hosts are unlikely to offer the same opportunities that allowed them to recover against the West Indies.Pakistan head into the upcoming Test series with Babar Azam back as their red-ball captain. His return to the leadership role produced mixed results in his first assignment, with Pakistan drawing their series against the West Indies 1-1.The hosts won the opening Test before Pakistan responded strongly in the second match, securing an eight-wicket victory to level the series.Despite that comeback, Pakistan's Test side continues to have concerns to address, particularly when playing away from home. Their struggles on overseas tours have also been reflected in their position in the World Test Championship standings.Pakistan slipped to the bottom of the WTC table after their defeat in the first Test against the West Indies. Their win in the following match helped them climb back to eighth position.The England series is expected to provide a significantly tougher examination. Conditions in England have traditionally posed problems for visiting sides, while Pakistan will also be under pressure to improve their WTC campaign.Akhtar believes England will be well aware of Pakistan's vulnerabilities and could prepare conditions specifically to test their batters."England won't make the same mistake West Indies did that allowed Pakistan to get into a winning position. They'll prepare seam-friendly conditions, which will be very difficult for Pakistan to handle," Akhtar said in a recent interview with a local sports platform, as quoted by Geo News.The former Pakistan pacer expects England to make full use of their home conditions rather than allow Pakistan to settle into the kind of position they reached in the second Test against the West Indies.Pakistan's recent overseas record adds further significance to the series. Their most recent Test victory away from home came against Sri Lanka in 2023, during Babar's first spell as captain.Babar subsequently stepped down from the leadership, with Shan Masood taking charge for nearly three years. However, Pakistan's difficulties outside home conditions continued during his tenure.Pakistan were beaten 3-0 in Australia before suffering a 2-0 series defeat in South Africa. They then lost 2-0 in Bangladesh, extending a disappointing run in overseas Tests.The results left Pakistan without an away Test victory for a prolonged period and underlined their difficulties in adapting to conditions outside the subcontinent.With Babar once again leading the Test side, the England tour will provide another opportunity for Pakistan to address those concerns. But Akhtar believes the challenge will be particularly demanding, with England expected to use seam-friendly conditions to put their batting under pressure.
Article Summary: Former Pakistan fast bowler Shoaib Akhtar has cautioned Pakistan about the challenge awaiting them in England. Pakistan head into the upcoming Test series with Babar Azam back as their red-ball captain. Akhtar believes England will be well aware of Pakistan's vulnerabilities and could prepare conditions specifically to test their batters.

Article Title: Ahead of Sri Lanka Tests, former all-rounder picks uncapped Gurnoor Brar as India's 'x-factor'
Article Text:
Gurnoor Brar (BCCI | X)

'He has the bounce, pace and fighting spirit': Maharoof backs Brar

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Maharoof backs 'quality player' Shubman Gill

India's squad for Sri Lanka Tests

India are set to begin their two-match Test series against Sri Lanka on August 15 in Galle, with former Sri Lankan all-rounder Farveez Maharoof backing uncapped pacer Gurnoor Brar to provide the visitors with an X-factor. Brar, who was included in India's squad for the Test series, made his international debut against Afghanistan in an ODI earlier this year. He has picked up 11 wickets in six innings at an average of 32.81.The 25-year-old also boasts impressive numbers in first-class cricket, having claimed 62 wickets in 19 matches at an average of 25.24. His record includes four four-wicket hauls, two five-wicket hauls and a 10-wicket match haul.Speaking to reporters during an interaction organised by Sony Sports Network, Maharoof singled out Brar as a potential game-changer for India."I like Gurnoor Brar. I think he can be an X-factor. He has the bounce, pace, the fighting spirit, and he can be nasty," Maharoof said.Brar impressed during India's warm-up game against Sri Lanka XI, finishing with three wickets and troubling several batters who have already featured in Test cricket."If you watched the warm-up match, some of the deliveries he bowled against the batters who have already played Tests, he made them quite uneasy. A couple of players also got some body blows," Maharoof said.The former Sri Lankan all-rounder admitted that Brar's lack of Test experience could make his selection a gamble, but believes his ability to generate pace and bounce could make him a valuable weapon in short spells."If I am the think tank of India, I will be tempted to try Brar. I know he has not played red-ball cricket and has just played white-ball cricket for India, but he brings that X-factor, those short spells where you just want to break the rhythm of the batter. He can be a lethal weapon," he added.Maharoof also reserved praise for India captain Shubman Gill, who will lead the side in the two-Test series."Shubman Gill is a quality player. He is one of the best going around; his Test average this year is 70-odd. Numbers speak for themselves. The way he batted in the second innings of that warm-up match was superb. He is one of the best going around, not only in Tests, but also in all formats," Maharoof said.Shubman Gill (Captain), KL Rahul (Vice-Captain), Yashasvi Jaiswal, Rishabh Pant (WK), Sarfaraz Khan, Dhruv Jurel (WK), Ravindra Jadeja, Kuldeep Yadav, Manav Suthar, Mohammed Siraj, Prasidh Krishna, Gurnoor Brar, Devdutt Padikkal, Saransh Jain and Auqib Nabi.
Article Summary: Farveez Maharoof backs Gurnoor Brar to provide India with an X-factor. Former Sri Lankan all-rounder backs 'quality player' Shubman Gill. India begin two- match Test series against Sri Lanka on August 15 in Galle.

Article Title: East Bengal face early Asian test against Al-Arabi in AFC Champions League 2 qualifier
Article Text:
Kolkata: East Bengal FC players (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: East Bengal’s new season is just three-match-old and the reigning ISL champions are already facing the grind of Asian football at a time when the team hardly looks to have started the ignition.On paper, stakes for Antonio Lopez Habas’s side in Wednesday’s AFC Champions League 2 qualifier against Al-Arabi SC at the Salt Lake Stadium have a kind of you-win-sone-you-lose-some feel. A win against the Kuwait Premier League runners-up will give East Bengal a direct place in group stage of the continent’s second-tier club football while a defeat will plummet them to the AFC Challenge League.However, the match is perhaps coming too soon for the new ISL winners to make the most of the situation and this is what is making Habas’ brow furrow with a sense of anxiety.Kick-starting the season with a loss to Mohun Bagan less than three weeks ago and following it with big wins against two novice challengers in the ongoing Durand Cup hardly creates a convincing look of a team ready to make a mark beyond the country’s boundary. Add to this the fact that the home team will enter the contest with only three foreigners, newcomers Daniel Ramirez and Chris Chris Ikonomidis as well as retained Mohammad Rashid, and it makes the case more demanding for East Bengal.Habas, during the pre-match news conference, tried to take the rough with the smooth. A lot will depend on the Anwar Ali-led all-Indian defence against a Kuwaiti side which has come here with its full foreign power and playing friendlies against top sides in Turkiye. In Palestinian striker Zaid Qunbar, Nigerian winger Anayo Iwuala and Brazilian Lucas Shallon, the visitors under Croatian coach Goran Sablic have both pace and potency in the attacking third.'We know that we are facing a very good team who will play in front of their fans. But we are here to play football and not focus on atmosphere," Sablic told reporters.However, given the nature of the one-off contest, East Bengal’s veteran Spanish coach won’t mind frustrating the opponents with a battle of attrition and dragging it to a likely tie-breaker. This is why, Jeakson Singh and Rashid could be employed as defensive midfielders ahead of their backline.“We didn’t have too much time for preparation (for this match). This may not be the best situation for us. But I hope we’ll deal with it with a tactical game and a 100% dedication from the players. The players have to sacrifice a lot, they need to be disciplined and perform well to live up to the challenge,” Habas pointed out.
Article Summary: East Bengal face Al-Arabi SC in AFC Champions League 2 qualifier on Wednesday. The reigning ISL champions are already facing the grind of Asian football at a time when the team hardly looks to have started the ignition. A win against the Kuwait Premier League runners-up will give East Bengal a direct place in group stage of the continent’s second-tier club football.

Article Title: India's U20 Wrestling team's Slovakia trip nearly hit by visa crisis over alleged human trafficking case
Article Text:
Representational photo of wrestling mats. (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: An alleged human trafficking episode involving an Indian sports team in Slovakia nearly put the country’s wrestling contingent’s trip to the U20 World Championships in Bratislava in jeopardy, with the Slovakia Embassy in Delhi initially refusing to process the visa applications.The crisis eased on Tuesday after intervention by United World Wrestling (UWW) and a written undertaking from the Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) assuring that the entire contingent would return to India after the tournament.The 45-member wrestling contingent spent nearly three weeks in uncertainty after the embassy linked the applications to an incident involving an Indian team — from abn unrelated sport — that travelled to Slovakia in June. The details of the support staff members of that team who reportedly went missing and did not return are not clear, with Slovak authorities allegedly investigating if they sought asylum.“The UWW told us that there was a case of human trafficking in which an unrelated Indian team from another sport had gone to Slovakia for a tournament in June and some support staff members went missing or were looking for asylum there and never returned to India.It was not related to wrestling,” a WFI source said.The federation had been pursuing the embassy since July 21 but received no response. It then approached UWW, which contacted the championship organisers and Slovak authorities. Following assurances from UWW, the embassy agreed to process the wrestlers’ applications and collect their biometrics.The WFI was also asked to furnish a written guarantee that all members of the contingent would return after the championships and, if required, assemble at the embassy for a headcount. “After the UWW assurance, the Slovakia embassy agreed to process the visas. The WFI was told to give a written undertaking stating that all our wrestlers and coaching support staff will assemble at the embassy, if need be, upon their return,” the source added.Biometrics of 42 members, including all 30 athletes, were completed on Tuesday, with interviews scheduled for Wednesday. The contingent includes 30 wrestlers, nine coaches, three referees and three physiotherapists. No managers will travel as they didn’t receive the govt’s financial approval.The first batch, including Greco-Roman wrestlers, is scheduled to leave Delhi on Aug 14. The championships will be held from Aug 16-23.
Article Summary: The 45-member wrestling contingent spent nearly three weeks in uncertainty. The crisis eased on Tuesday after intervention by United World Wrestling. The embassy linked the applications to an incident involving an Indian team that travelled to Slovakia in June. The details of the support staff members of that team who reportedly went missing and did not return are not clear.

Article Title: Indian para-cyclists shine at UCI Parasport Denmark Grand Prix with 12-medal haul
Article Text:
Indian para-cyclists shine in Denmark

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Indian para-cyclists put up an impressive show at the UCI Parasport Denmark Grand Prix in Odense, held from Aug 7 to 9, returning with a rich haul of 12 medals, including two gold, five silver and five bronze. Seventeen-year-old Gujarat cyclist Vishwa Vasani (WC3) was among the standout performers, winning four bronze medals in the 1km Individual Time Trial (ITT), Scratch Race, 200m Sprint and Elimination Race.Paralympian Arshad Shaikh (MC2) was India's most successful cyclist at the event, claiming six medals — two gold, three silver and one bronze, across various track events. His performances underlined his consistency on the international circuit.Sixteen-year-old Anshuman (MC1) added two silver medals to India's tally, marking another promising performance by one of the country's emerging para-cyclists.The combined effort of the three cyclists earned India a 12-medal haul and highlighted the country's growing presence in international para-cycling.All three cyclists train under chief coach Aditya Mehta, who has played a key role in identifying, developing and preparing Indian para-cyclists for international competitions.The performances in Odense also offered further evidence of the depth of talent emerging in Indian para-cycling, with experienced campaigners and young prospects making their mark on the international stage.
Article Summary: Indian para-cyclists put up an impressive show at the UCI Parasport Denmark Grand Prix in Odense. India returned with a rich haul of 12 medals, including two gold, five silver and five bronze. Paralympian Arshad Shaikh (MC2) was India's most successful cyclist at the event, claiming six medals.

Article Title: 'It's time to step into the top eight': Sjoerd Marijne sets target for Indian Women's Hockey
Article Text:
TOI Interview: Sjoerd Marijne

How has it been so far with the practice, training and preparations?

You have been back with the team for several months now. How different is this group from the one you coached at the Tokyo Olympics?

India have often shown that they can compete with the best, but consistency has sometimes been an issue. Your thoughts on that.

What are the areas in which you have seen the biggest improvement in the team?

With players coming from different backgrounds and having different levels of experience, how have you managed to make them function as a team?

You have a very experienced squad. How do you see the role of the senior players at the World Cup?

There are 11 World Cup debutants in the team. What has impressed you most about the youngsters?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

If India are to go deep into the World Cup, what quality do you believe this team needs to have?

Specialist support brought in by Marijne:

July 30-Aug 2; Aug 4-24: Goalkeeping sessions with the former Netherlands goalkeeper Pirmin Blaak, who also worked on penalty corner defence.

Aug 4-31: A dedicated drag-flicking camp with the former Dutch international Taeke Taekema.

Aug 6-7 & 9-12: Mental training sessions with Ben Wienk aimed at helping players prepare for the pressures of the World Cup.

The Indian women’s hockey team has proved it can punch above its weight. Now, chief coach Sjoerd Marijne wants consistency as India target a place in the world’s top eight. The Dutchman, who returned as head coach earlier this year, spoke to TOI about the team’s preparations, its changing dynamics, the role of seniors and youngsters, and the need for greater consistency, ahead of Sunday’s World Cup opener against China. Excerpts:We are happy. We played Australia, Japan and Chile, and we have a practice match against Netherlands. It’s good to work on the final details and see what we want to improve. We are very focused on ourselves and not being too busy with the opponents or thinking about what we need to do against them.We have more young players than in the past, and they have developed really well. Of course, the older players have more international experience. They have played in Pro League, the World Cup two seasons ago, and have had all kinds of experiences. Also, more girls speak English now, which is very good. That helps me a lot.That is something we are working towards. As I said earlier, we are the best of the rest. We have proven that with the Nations Cup, and now it’s time to make the step into the top eight in the world. But that will come with ups and downs. Winning against teams like Australia and England, the top eight teams, and doing that consistently — not just once — will be our biggest challenge.One important factor in building a team is discipline. We have certain values and rules in the team, and you have to follow those rules. I see that this has improved. You can see it, for instance, in the matches against New Zealand in the Nations Cup. We were very disciplined until the end of the match, and that is a very big improvement.The most important thing is that they play for the same flag. It doesn’t matter where they come from — which state, district or whatever. They all come from India. It is about knowing your role in the team and taking that responsibility. In a team, you don’t always have to be each other’s best friends. But you have to respect each other and help each other.The role of the experienced players is to set an example — to show how to win matches, how to behave, how to play without fear and those kinds of things. It is difficult for the seniors because they always have to give the right example. They are setting the standards, and I always want those standards to be really, really high.Their technical and dribbling skills are very, very good. They learn fast. But the main thing I expect from them is that they play freely. They don’t think so much; they just want to play hockey. They can make mistakes — that happens, and it’s normal at that age. But I don’t want to see them not running or not making a tackle.We need to execute our chances. In the Nations Cup, in every match we got an average of five to 10 chances, but we scored one or two. We had a very high conversion rate from penalty corners. If you play against China, you may get three or four chances. You have to make them count. Besides that, we need structured and disciplined defence.Sjoerd Marijne has brought in specialist coaches to work on different aspects of the Indian team’s game in the build-up to and during the World Cup. Speaking about it, he said, “I trust the coaches and I know their qualities. They know things that I don’t know.”
Article Summary: Chief coach Sjoerd Marijne spoke to TOI about the team’s preparations, its changing dynamics, the role of seniors and youngsters, and the need for greater consistency. India face China in their World Cup opener on Sunday.

Article Title: Parthib Gogoi's brace, Ajaraie's sixth goal help NorthEast United storm into Durand Cup quarterfinals
Article Text:
Caption: Parthiv Gogoi with teammates after scoring in Guwahati on Tuesday (Credit: Durand Cup Media)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: NorthEast United continued their winning march into the knockout stage of 135th edition of Durand Cup with a dominant 3-1 win over debutants FC1 on Tuesday. Adding to the good news for the home crowd at Indira Gandhi Athletic Stadium in Guwahati, their local poster boy, Parthib Gogoi, rose to the occasion with a brace, even as NEUFC star striker Alaaeddine Ajaraie kept up his scoring touch with his sixth goal in three group games.The win meant that the Highlanders ended the group stage on top of Group F with nine points and eased their way into the quarterfinals while staying on course for a successful title defence. The newcomers from Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, however, lost their chance for a knockout berth in their debut season and stayed behind second-placed Bodoland FC, with the same three points but a worse goal difference. They also played one game more than the Assam club.FC1, who claimed a historic win on debut against Karbi Anglong Morning Star FC, almost got a breakthrough in the seventh minute through a penalty. But Ahmed Quereshi was denied by debutant NEUFC goalkeeper K Mohanraj with a low diving save.The Highlanders punished them four minutes later after a well-worked move involving Spanish debutant Antonio Moyano and Jithin MS — making his 100th appearance for NEUFC — with the ball falling to an unmarked Gogoi at the back post, who calmly slotted it in.The lead was doubled nine minutes after the restart as Moyano’s dangerous free-kick was headed towards goal by Eneko Satrustegui, who found Gogoi once again in the right place at the right time to guide the ball in with ease. Gogoi played provider for the third goal as his precise through ball fell into the path of Ajaraie, who calmly chipped the ball over the onrushing goalkeeper in the 68th minute.FC1 did find a consolation goal — and the only one conceded by NEUFC so far — three minutes later through Mohammed Ilyas, but could not find a way to extend their stay in their maiden season at the tournament. Meanwhile, in the evening fixture in Shillong, Nongkseh SS&CC routed Mumbay FC 7-0 at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium to end the miserable run of the Mumbai newcomers in Durand Cup.Hardy Cliff Nongbri and Dawancha Carlos Challam both struck twice, while Kitboklang Pale, Chesterpoul Lyngdoh and Sheen Stevenson were also on the scoresheet as the third-placed Shillong club kept alive their slim chance of qualification.They have four points from three games and will closely watch rivals and second-placed Langsning FC’s performance in their last group encounter.
Article Summary: NorthEast United continued their winning march into the knockout stage of 135th edition of Durand Cup with a dominant 3-1 win over debutants FC1 on Tuesday. Parthib Gogoi scored a brace, even as NEUFC star striker Alaaeddine Ajaraie kept up his scoring touch with his sixth goal in three group games.

Article Title: India's 11 World Cup debutants: Deepika, Shilpi's remarkable journeys to Hockey's biggest stage
Article Text:
Photo caption: Deepika Soreng (left) and Shilpi Dabas with her parents (Credit: TOI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

WC debutants:

When the Indian women’s team opens its World Cup campaign against China on Sunday, 11 players in the squad will be making their World Cup debuts. They come from different corners of the country — Mizoram, Jharkhand, Odisha, Haryana, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab — and have taken different paths to reach hockey’s biggest stage.Some grew up with the sport, others took it up after playing different sports, while for some, hockey became a route to a better life. One of them is Jharkhand’s Deepika Soreng, who grew up in Simdega district and was introduced to hockey by Father Benedict Kujur at RC Upgraded Middle School in Karangaguri, where students were required to bring a hockey stick to school.Life, however, was far from certain. Deepika’s father died when she was a child, leaving her mother, Friska, to take up whatever work she could to support her daughter and two sons.“When I later got a chance to join the residential academy in Simdega, my mother went to Rourkela to work at the steel plant,” said Deepika, one of three students of late coach Pratima Barwa — alongside Salima Tete and Beauty Dungdung — who will play at the World Cup.Friska spent more than a decade working at the steel plant, living away from her children so they could continue their education and pursue their dreams. Years later, after Deepika broke into the national team and secured a job with the Railways, she was finally able to bring her mother back home.Friska now lives in Ranchi in her daughter’s apartment. “Next, I would like to take my mother somewhere by air. She has never travelled by flight, and I really want her to experience that at least once,” Deepika said.Because of the circumstances, Friska has not been able to follow her daughter’s hockey journey closely. She knows Deepika plays hockey and represents India, but herself knows little about the game itself. In another corner of the country, Anita Dabas, however, has closely followed her daughter Shilpi’s every step as she tried to break into the national team. A former national player from Haryana who also represented Air India, Anita made it to the India camp around 30 years ago.“She couldn’t make the team eventually. But now Shilpi has got that opportunity to represent India at the World Cup and it feels like the dream of the entire family has come true,” Shilpi’s father Anil, told TOI from their home in Sonipat. For Shilpi, the wait has been agonising. She has been playing senior nationals since 2018, but it was only earlier this year that she finally received a call-up to the senior national camp following her performance in Women’s Hockey India League with SG Pipers.“I had been trying for many years. Whenever there was a national selection or tournament, I would think, ‘Maybe my name will come this time.’ I would feel that surely it would happen now, but it just wasn’t happening,” the 28-year-old told TOI from Netherlands. There were moments of frustration, but Shilpi never stopped working. Her parents and coach Pritam Siwach ensured she kept going through the difficult years.“She would get irritated and frustrated at times. There were many occasions when I had to motivate her,” said Pritam.The persistence has now paid off. Shilpi has not only sealed her place in the World Cup squad but also played a major role in India’s Nations Cup triumph in June. Anil credits the Haryana state association and her first coach, Rajinder Singh Sr., a member of India’s 1980 Moscow Olympics gold medal-winning squad, for playing important roles in her development. Pratima did much the same for Deepika, guiding her for almost a decade before her death last year. Deepika, however, will carry her coach’s memory when she takes the field on Sunday, as will Salima and Beauty.And while they will share the same World Cup stage, the journeys that brought Deepika and Shilpi there could hardly have been more different. They were on two very different paths leading to the same dream.Lalthantluangi, Shilpi Dabas, Ishika Chaudhary, Sakshi Rana, Sunelita Toppo, Deepika Soreng, DeepikaRutuja Dadaso Pisal, Ishika, Baljeet Kaur, Beauty Dungdung
Article Summary: 11 players in the squad will be making their World Cup debuts. They come from different corners of the country. Some grew up with the sport, others took it up after playing different sports. For some, hockey became a route to a better life. Deepika Soreng's father died when she was a child.

Article Title: From jumping a fence to World silver, 19-yr-old Basant Meghwal scripts history
Article Text:
Basant Meghwal (Image credit: X)

JAIPUR: For someone whose journey into athletics began under accidental circumstances — jumping over a fence while bunking school in his remote border Rajasthan village — Basant Kumar Meghwal’s silver effort at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon then is an extraordinary leap of faith.In what is proving a breakout season for the youngster, the 19-year-old Meghwal scripted history on Saturday by becoming the first Indian athlete to win a world high jump medal. He had also clinched gold at the Asian Under-20 Athletics Championships earlier this year.In Eugene, the podium finishers all maxed out at a height of 2.21 meters, meaning final placements were decided entirely by countback rules based on missed attempts. Algeria’s Younes Ayachi clinched gold by clearing the bar cleanly on his first attempt. Basant secured a momentous, personal-best silver for India by clearing the height on his second run, while Great Britain's Otis Poole took bronze on his third and final try.Meghwal’s run-up, though, begins differently. Not long ago, when he was in a field in his hamlet in Anupgarh tehsil of Sriganganagar district, lolling about the cattle instead of being in school, he spotted his physical training instructor, Iqbal Singh Maan, passing by.Fearing he would be caught skipping school, Basant leaped cleanly over a wire fence to hide.“His teacher saw that leap, immediately recognised his raw talent, and asked him to come to school instead. After that, he began to train him for the high jump,” father Gangaram Meghwal told TOI.“Before this happened, we didn't even know what high jump was or that such a sport existed.”The path to international glory required considerable sacrifices from the family. “We still carry a debt of around 3.5 lakh rupees because sports expenses are extremely high,” Meghwal Sr said, “I am a daily wage driver without any land of my own, earning around Rs 12,000-13,000 a month to raise my two children. I took loans from relatives and private lenders to finance Basant’s training, proper diet, and equipment.Just a single pair of high jump shoes costs Rs 15,000.”Despite the financial burden, Gangaram kept his son’s focus firmly on his craft. “I told him not to worry about the money, the loans will eventually be paid off. Focus on making a name for yourself. Today, seeing our child achieve a world medal brings us immense happiness,” said the proud father.Son Basant now represents the Indian Navy, a career move made through the sports quota entry. “When he started performing well, people guided us that it would secure his future,” his father added, “It changed everything for him, as it gave him a stable job and allowed him to pursue his athletic career without worrying about basic sustenance.”
Article Summary: Basant Kumar Meghwal won silver at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon. The 19-year-old became the first Indian athlete to win a world high jump medal. He had also clinched gold at the Asian Under-20 Athletics Championships earlier this year.

NEW DELHI: India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak believes the team gained more from its warm-up match against Sri Lanka than it could have from several additional days of conventional training, as the visitors completed a six-wicket win ahead of the Test series.Team India wrapped up its only practice fixture before the two-match series with a successful 207-run chase, giving players from both departments valuable match time ahead of the opening Test in Galle from August 15.Kotak was particularly impressed by the intensity on display, saying the competitive nature of the fixture made it more valuable than routine practice sessions.Speaking in a video shared by the BCCI on X, Kotak said: “I think it was very good, very productive because if we practice four more days, I don't think it will be as good as the practice match because the bowlers bowled with good intensity. Article Title: Pratapgarh’s Shahnavaz scripts history, wins bronze at U-20 worlds
Article Text:
Shahnavaz Khan

LUCKNOW: Pratapgarh’s Shahnavaz Khan has become the first Indian man to win a long jump medal at the World Athletics U-20 Championships at Eugene, the US. Shaili Singh won silver in the women’s long jump in 2021. Shahnavaz clinched bronze in the men’s long jump with a best effort of 7.84m.Speaking to TOI from the US, an elated Shahnavaz said his athletics journey began near a canal in Sangrampur village in Pratapgarh, where he trained with local children and friends under senior athlete Mohd Hadees Khan.The 19-year-old said he later moved to Mumbai during the Covid period after taking admission to Pillai College of Engineering in Panvel. There, he trained under coach Imzamam-ul-Haq for two years before shifting in 2024 to the Sports Authority of India (SAI) centre in Trivandrum, where he is currently based.Reflecting on his achievement, Shahnavaz said he was aware of the significance of the medal. “I knew that before today, no Indian had ever won a medal in the men’s long jump category at the U-20 World Championship. This medal is not just mine, it belongs to the country.I am going to the Asian Games in September, and I will finish on the podium there,” he said.Shahnavaz added that he was unable to produce his personal best because of fitness concerns. “I had an injury on my right side and was also dealing with cramps, so I could not deliver my personal best. Just last month in July, I won gold at the Junior Asian Athletics Championships with the same mark of 7.84, and today I achieved 7.84 again.My personal best is 8.30, which I recorded at the Inter-State Athletics Championship,” he said.The athlete credited his uncle, Sharukh, a steeplechase runner, as a major source of inspiration. “My motivation to win medals comes from my uncle, Sharukh, who is a steeplechase athlete. He set a record last year, and whenever he returned with a medal, it inspired me and made me feel that I would bring one home too,” Khan said.UP Athletics Association secretary Narendra praised Shahnavaz Khan. He said, “My best wishes are with the athletes. They put up good results on the wall.”
Article Summary: Pratapgarh’s Shahnavaz Khan has become the first Indian man to win a long jump medal at the World Athletics U-20 Championships at Eugene, the US. The 19-year- old clinched bronze in the men's long jump with a best effort of 7.84m. He trained under coach Imzamam-ul-Haq for two years.

Article Title: World Athletics U20 Championships: India end campaign with three-medal haul
Article Text:
L-R: Basant Kumar Meghwal, Ashish Yadav and Shahnavaz Khan (AFI Photos)

India finish with two silver, one bronze

India continue to build U20 medal record

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India's campaign at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Oregon, USA, ended with three medals after high jumper Pooja Singh finished seventh in the women's final, falling well short of the national senior record that had raised expectations around her title bid.The 19-year-old Pooja could clear only 1.84m in the final and failed in all three attempts at 1.87m. Her performance was below the 1.93m national senior record she set while winning gold at the Asian U20 Athletics Championships in May.Pooja, who is also the reigning Senior Asian Athletics Championships gold medallist, had entered the competition as one of India's leading medal hopes.Australia's Izobelle Louison-Roe won the gold with a clearance of 1.92m. Hungary's Lilianna Batori and Spain's Aitana Alonso both cleared 1.90m, with Batori taking silver and Alonso bronze.India's women's 4x400m relay team also ended its campaign with a ninth-place finish in the final. Bhoomika Nehate, Tahura Khatun, Tanu Chaudhary and Thiya Arumugam clocked 3:45.28 to finish last.The United States won gold in 3:29.15, followed by Australia (3:31.39) and Great Britain (3:32.08).India's three-medal haul comprised two silver and one bronze, matching the country's medal tally from the 2021 and 2022 editions of the championships.Ashish Yadav opened India's medal count with silver in the men's javelin throw, before Basant Kumar Meghwal added another silver in the men's high jump. Shahnavaz Khan then secured bronze in the men's long jump.While the campaign ended without a gold medal, the three-medal haul underlined India's improved consistency at the global junior level.Between 2002 and 2018, India won only four medals at the World Athletics U20 Championships. Those included historic gold medals from Neeraj Chopra in the men's javelin throw in 2016 and Hima Das in the women's 400m in 2018.Discus thrower Seema Antil won India's first medal at the championships, taking silver in 2002, while Navjeet Kaur Dhillon added bronze in the same event in 2014.India subsequently won three medals in 2021, including silver medals for Amit in the men's 10,000m race walk and Shaili Singh in the women's long jump, besides a bronze in the mixed 4x400m relay.The 2022 edition brought three more medals, with Selva Prabhu Thirumaran and the mixed 4x400m relay team winning silver and Rupal Chaudhary taking bronze.India managed only one medal in the 2024 edition, with Aarti winning bronze in the women's 10,000m race walk.The three-medal haul in the latest edition therefore represents a return to the stronger medal returns of 2021 and 2022.
Article Summary: India finish with two silver, one bronze at World Athletics U20 Championships. High jumper Pooja Singh fails to clear 1.84m in the women's final. India's women's 4x400m relay team also finishes ninth in the final.

Article Title: Sarfaraz Khan or Dhruv Jurel? India's no. 6 dilemma takes centre stage ahead of Sri Lanka Test
Article Text:
Dhruv Jurel and Sarfaraz Khan. (AFP Photo)

Sarfaraz or Jurel for No. 6?

What will the bowling attack look like?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

As Team India sweats it out ahead of the first Test against Sri Lanka at the Galle International Stadium from Saturday, the biggest contest may not be against the Islanders but within the dressing room itself. The arrival of chief selector Ajit Agarkar in Colombo on Tuesday underlines the importance of the decisions that await the team management.With India’s World Test Championship hopes hanging in the balance, getting the playing XI right could be the difference between staying in contention for a place in the final and seeing the remainder of the cycle turn into a mere formality. The key questions revolve around the middle order and the bowling attack.The selection debate that has generated the most discussion centres on the No. 6 position. Devdutt Padikkal’s unbeaten 142 in the warm-up game has virtually sealed the No. 3 slot vacated by the injured Sai Sudharsan. That leaves the management with a straight choice between Sarfaraz Khan and Dhruv Jurel. Former India wicketkeeper and ex-chief selector Kiran More believes Jurel’s previous Test experience may give him the edge.“I think Jurel will play ahead of Sarfaraz because he has already played Test cricket and done well. He’s a good fielder too. Sarfaraz has come in later and will get opportunities,” More told TOI.Jurel’s overall record is respectable. In 10 Tests, he has scored 478 runs at 34.14, including a century and a fifty. However, the concern is not just the numbers but the manner of his dismissals, especially against spin.His recent outings have done little to strengthen his case. After shining in the unofficial Test against South Africa A, Jurel struggled in the subsequent Test series, returning scores of 14, 13, 0 and 2. Veteran off-spinner Simon Harmer repeatedly exposed his vulnerability, dismissing him in both innings of each Test.The trend continued in Sri Lanka. Jurel managed scores of one and 17 in the warm-up match and was dismissed cheaply by off-spinner Ramesh Mendis. On a Galle track that is expected to turn, India’s think tank will be wary of taking a batter into the series with visible doubts against spin.Former India batter Mohammad Kaif feels Sarfaraz should be the preferred choice. “If India stick to backing players who have already been around the side, then Jurel could get the nod. But if you ask me for the best XI, Sarfaraz is in it because of his ability against spin,” Kaif said on his YouTube channel. Few Indian batters have built their reputation against spin as convincingly as Sarfaraz. His first-class record is extraordinary. He averages 64.73 with 5,114 runs and 17 centuries in 62 matches.The other dilemma concerns India’s bowling combination. Mohammed Siraj and Prasidh Krishna look certain to lead the pace attack in the opening Test. The bigger question is whether India opt for a third seamer or strengthen the spin department. Conventional wisdom suggests Sri Lankan pitches favour spin, but former India left-arm pacer Irfan Pathan believes seamers can also be effective.“Whenever I played in Sri Lanka, there was always a bit more zip in the wickets. In humid conditio-ns, the ball also tends to move arou-nd,” Pathan had told TOI recently.Kiran More expects India to field three pacers unless Galle produces an outright raging turner.“My three seamers would be Siraj, Krishna and Gurnoor Brar. Since Nitish Kumar Reddy is unavailable, India need that extra pace option,” More said. If More’s formula is followed, Ravindra Jadeja and Kuldeep Yadav would operate as the two frontline spinners.
Article Summary: India's World Test Championship hopes hanging in the balance. The key questions revolve around the middle order and the bowling attack. Devdutt Padikkal’s unbeaten 142 in the warm-up game has virtually sealed the No. 3 slot vacated by Sai Sudharsan. That leaves the management with a straight choice between Sarfaraz Khan and Dhruv Jurel.

Article Title: Washington Sundar's Sri Lanka Test availability in doubt, chances of joining team 'very slim'

NEW DELHI: After losing Jasprit Bumrah and Sai Sudharsan due to injuries, it has emerged that there's a big question mark over Washington Sundar's availability for the second Test. The selectors had picked Washington only for the second Test since he is recovering from a hamstring injury.TOI understands that the Centre of Excellence (CoE) and Indian team management would want to exercise caution with Washington after the spate of injuries in the team. "At this moment, the chances of Washington going to Sri Lanka are very slim. The team management has been told to plan accordingly. The BCCI medical team is wary of pushing him into a Test match. There have been a few instances where players have broken down immediately after recovering from an injury," a BCCI source told TOI."Washington was picked only for the second Test knowing it will be touch-and-go for him to gain full fitness. He hasn't played much after sustaining the injury in England last month. His workload is being carefully increased," the source added.It is learnt that the selectors are unlikely to name a replacement if Washington is officially ruled out.The selectors have already named a 15-member squad. "Washington will be the 16th member if links up with the team. It needs to be assessed if it will be worthwhile to send him for a Test match without any game time. A thorough assessment will be done next week which will include how the team is placed in Sri Lanka,” the source said.No timeline for Bumrah, Akash Deep yetTOI has also learnt that the medical team at the CoE hasn't set any timeline for the return of pacers Bumrah and Akash Deep. Bumrah is nursing a knee injury which he suffered in England last month while Akash Deep has been out of action from Jan due to a stress fracture in the back."The CoE was working on increasing Bumrah's workload before the Test series in Sri Lanka. It was felt that he would not be ready in time. It has been a long time since he has bowled in longer formats for a while. The CoE is very careful about him. They haven't given any timeline on him.Anyway, Indian cricket may have to now start getting ready for life without Bumrah especially in the longer formats after next year," the source said."For Akash Deep, the CoE's target was to get him cricket fit by the Sri Lanka tour. That hasn't happened. Now, they haven't communicated any timeline to the team management and the selection committee. It's not easy to come back from a back injury. The team management hopes that he will be available for the tour of New Zealand which will be very crucial. It will be a boost for the team if both Bumrah and Akash are available for the two Tests in New Zealand," the source added.

It is learnt that the selectors are unlikely to name a replacement if Washington is officially ruled out. Former Pakistan fast bowler Shoaib Akhtar has warned the Babar Azam-led side to be prepared for tough conditions during their upcoming three-Test series against England.The first Test will begin at Headingley in Leeds on August 19. Article Title: After being denied a direct spot, how can West Indies qualify for the 2027 ODI World Cup?
Article Text:
West Indies Cricket Team (AP Photo)

The route West Indies must navigate

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why West Indies cannot afford another slip

NEW DELHI: For a team with two ODI World Cup titles, West Indies have found themselves in an unfamiliar position again. The Caribbean side will not qualify automatically for the 2027 World Cup and must now negotiate the qualifying route to make the tournament in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.It is the third straight World Cup cycle in which West Indies have been pushed into the qualifiers, underlining the difficult road the former champions now face.The immediate challenge is the 2027 World Cup Qualifier in February, where West Indies will be joined by Ireland, four teams from the Cricket World Cup League 2 and four sides emerging from the Qualifier Playoff.West Indies cannot secure one of the automatic qualification spots before the September 30 cut-off. They are currently 10th in the ODI rankings, and even two victories over India before the deadline would not be enough to move them into the required bracket.That leaves the Qualifier as their route into the World Cup.The tournament carries an important incentive: win it, and West Indies go straight into the second round of the 2027 World Cup.But finishing between second and fourth would leave them with another hurdle.Those three teams will enter the first round of the World Cup, the Super Series, alongside another Qualifier team. Only the winner of that stage will progress to the second round.In other words, West Indies have little room for error. Winning the Qualifier would provide the cleanest route, while anything less could mean another high-pressure battle for survival.The Caribbean side already know what happens when the Qualifier campaign goes wrong.West Indies failed to make the 2023 World Cup through direct qualification and subsequently finished fifth in the Super Six stage of the Qualifier. The result was historic for the wrong reasons: they missed a World Cup for the first time.The consequences extended beyond that tournament. West Indies also failed to feature in the 2025 Champions Trophy, a competition they had not played since 2013.Now, with another World Cup qualification campaign ahead, the former two-time champions face a familiar test. This time, the objective is simple: navigate the qualifiers successfully and ensure they are back on cricket's biggest ODI stage in 2027.
Article Summary: West Indies will not qualify automatically for the 2027 World Cup. Caribbean side must now negotiate the qualifying route to make the tournament in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. It is the third straight World Cup cycle in which West Indies have been pushed into the qualifiers.

Who is Abhishek Porel?

Bengal cricketer Abhishek Porel, who plays for Delhi Capitals in the IPL, was arrested by police in Hooghly district on Monday night following a complaint by a woman alleging that he had sexual relations with her on the promise of marriage, news agency PTI reported on Tuesday."There was a case lodged against him and a court order to arrest him. He was arrested late last night. He will be produced in court today," Hooghly (Rural) Superintendent of Police Kunar Bhushan Singh was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.Porel was arrested by Mogra police and is expected to be produced before a court in Chinsurah later on Tuesday.Police have registered a case against Porel under several sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including Section 69, as well as provisions of the Information Technology Act, police sources said.A woman medical student from Karnataka filed a complaint against Porel at Mogra police station on June 23. He has played 32 First-Class, 23 List A and 61 T20 matches, scoring 1,408, 833 and 1,590 runs respectively.He has represented Bengal in the Ranji Trophy, Vijay Hazare Trophy and Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy.In his 32 First-Class matches, Porel has scored 1,408 runs at an average of 31.28. In 23 List A matches, he has made 833 runs at a strike rate of 95.63 and an average of 43.84.

Article Title: ‘For now, I am the captain’: Shaheen Afridi responds to Babar Azam captaincy reports ahead of 2027 ODI World Cup
Article Text:
File Pic: Babar Azam and Shaheen Afridi (Image credit: AFP)

Afridi shifts focus to World Cup preparations

Captaincy uncertainty hangs over Pakistan

Pakistan ODI captain Shaheen Shah Afridi has offered a pointed response when asked whether he will remain at the helm for next year's ODI World Cup, saying, “For now, I am the captain.”Afridi's comments come amid fresh speculation over Pakistan's leadership structure, with reports suggesting that former captain Babar Azam could eventually be handed the leadership across formats. With Pakistan having frequently changed captains in recent years, Afridi's tenure has come under scrutiny despite being appointed ODI skipper only last year.Speaking at a press conference with the captains of the National Champions Cup teams, Afridi was asked whether the Pakistan Cricket Board had confirmed that he would continue as captain through the 2027 World Cup.“For now, I am the captain,” Afridi replied.Rather than dwell on the uncertainty surrounding his position, Afridi turned his attention to the National Champions Cup, which runs from August 11 to 18 and features Pakistan's leading domestic players.The left-arm pacer believes the tournament can play an important role in building the depth Pakistan will need ahead of the World Cup.“Whenever we go to a World Cup, we face a lot of injuries. In case there are any injuries before the World Cup, we will already have players available.The tournament pool will make it easier for us to find replacements,” Afridi said.He also stressed the importance of allowing players to perform in their preferred roles.“This tournament will give everyone an opportunity to play according to their respective positions,” he said.Afridi believes performances in the competition could directly influence Pakistan's World Cup planning, with both form and fitness set to be monitored.“All the players will try to put in good performances. As I said, our focus is on the World Cup. Besides individual performances, the performances and fitness of other players will also be assessed,” he said.Afridi was appointed Pakistan's ODI captain in October 2025, replacing Mohammad Rizwan. However, Pakistan's leadership structure has remained unsettled, with Babar reportedly back in contention for a larger leadership role.Reports have suggested that the PCB could eventually make Babar an all-format captain, although there has been no official confirmation of such a move.Afridi, meanwhile, has stressed that his immediate focus remains on leading the side and preparing for the World Cup.Pakistan have a busy schedule ahead of the 2027 ODI World Cup, including tri-series commitments and a five-match series in England. The upcoming domestic competition will give the selectors another opportunity to assess the depth available to Afridi and identify potential replacements should injuries strike.
Article Summary: Pakistan ODI captain Shaheen Shah Afridi says, 'For now, I am the captain' Comments come amid fresh speculation over Pakistan's leadership structure. Babar Azam reportedly back in contention for a larger leadership role. Pakistan's National Champions Cup runs from August 11 to 18.

Article Title: Rajasthan stuck in 2012, Manipur in 2023: How actively are states with CWG medals promoting sports?
Article Text:
Are sports bodies of Indian states promoting the game properly?

Medal tally of India's athletes by birth state/UT

Haryana: Hit on the podium, not so much off it

Manipur still talking about 2023

Rajasthan: 14 years and counting

Uttar Pradesh and Delhi carry the same gloomy picture

And then come Tamil Nadu and others

The ones somewhere in the middle

How active are states/UTs with CWG medallists in promoting sport

Does it matter so much?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Social media presence Local sports events Government funding 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi interacted with India's CWG 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday. (Pic credit: PM Modi's X post)

Mirabai recalls four years of struggle

‘One family will bring three medals’

India’s Glasgow success

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hosted medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg. Modi heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.
